lesson.title: The event horizon: can light escape?
lesson.objective: Explain why light still travels at its usual local speed inside an event horizon, yet cannot reach an observer outside.
lesson.approachReason: Testing the claim that a black hole slows light to a stop reveals the more useful idea: the horizon marks where outward escape paths end.

blocks.heading: Light does not slow to a stop
blocks.body: An astronaut beside the flashlight measures its beam moving at the speed of light, even after crossing the event horizon. The horizon is not a wall that catches the beam. It is a boundary: once inside, even light aimed outward has no future path that leads back outside.
blocks.example: A brighter flashlight sends more light, not faster light.

hints: Think about the beam's speed beside the astronaut, not whether it reaches a distant telescope.
Crossing the horizon changes the beam's possible destinations, not its locally measured speed.
blocks.retry: Separate what happens nearby from where the beam can eventually go. Locally it moves at light speed; globally it cannot escape.

blocks.heading: A boundary between possible destinations
blocks.body: For an outward-pointing flash just outside the horizon, a path to a distant observer is still possible. At the horizon, an outward-directed light ray cannot move out beyond it; inside, even that ray remains inside. This is why the event horizon is called a point of no return—not because light stops moving, but because no signal from inside can get out.

hints: Both probes aim their flashes directly outward.
Compare the possible destinations of light starting just outside and just inside.
blocks.retry: The question is not whether a flashlight works near a black hole. It is which side of the boundary the flash starts on.

hints: Imagine replacing one outward-going light ray with a million.
Would any of those rays start on the other side of the horizon?
blocks.retry: Adding power changes how much light is sent. It does not create a route from inside the horizon to outside.

blocks.heading: Replace the mistaken picture
blocks.prompt: A friend says, “Nothing escapes because gravity makes light stop at the horizon.” In your own words, give them a better explanation.
blocks.model: Light never stops in a nearby observer's measurement. The event horizon is the boundary beyond which even an outward-directed light signal has no future path to the outside.

activities.title: A flashlight just inside
activities.prompt: An astronaut crosses a black hole's event horizon and immediately points a flashlight outward. Why can't its beam reach a distant observer?
activities.reveal: The beam does not slow to a stop. Inside the horizon, even light aimed outward cannot follow a future path back outside.

options.text: The beam moves at light speed nearby, but its path cannot lead outside.
options.feedback: Yes. Local speed and eventual destination are different questions.

options.text: Gravity slows the beam to a complete stop at the horizon.
options.feedback: An observer beside the beam still measures it moving at light speed.

options.text: The beam escapes if the flashlight is powerful enough.
options.feedback: More power produces more light, not a path out of the horizon.

options.text: The beam bounces off the horizon like a solid surface.
options.feedback: The event horizon is a boundary, not a physical surface.

activities.title: Slide across the horizon
activities.prompt: Place a flashlight at different distances from the center of an idealized black hole. At each position, it fires a beam directly outward. Which positions give the beam a route to a distant observer? A distance of 1 horizon radius marks the event horizon.
activities.reveal: Just outside, the outward beam has a route away; just inside, it does not. Its locally measured speed is still the speed of light at either position.

bands.title: Inside
bands.detail: Even a directly outward beam has no route to an observer outside.

bands.title: At the horizon
bands.detail: An outward-directed light ray cannot move out beyond the boundary.

bands.title: Outside
bands.detail: A directly outward beam can travel toward a distant observer.

activities.title: Follow each beam
activities.prompt: Tap the two flashlight nodes, then trace their connections. Which beam has a route to the distant telescope?
activities.reveal: The outside beam can connect to the distant telescope. The inside beam still travels, but every part of its future route stays inside.

nodes.label: Flashlight outside
nodes.detail: It fires directly away from the black hole, starting beyond the horizon.

nodes.label: Outside beam
nodes.detail: This outward-going light can continue away from the black hole.

nodes.label: Distant telescope
nodes.detail: An outward-going signal from outside can reach an observer far away.

nodes.label: Event horizon
nodes.detail: This boundary separates starting points that can send an outward beam away from those that cannot.

nodes.label: Flashlight inside
nodes.detail: It also fires directly outward, but starts inside the boundary.

nodes.label: Inside beam
nodes.detail: It moves at light speed locally, yet cannot cross outward through the horizon.

nodes.label: Future inside
nodes.detail: The beam's future remains within the black hole.

questions.question: After crossing the event horizon, an astronaut switches on a flashlight and measures its beam beside them. Which description fits?
options: The beam moves at light speed nearby, though it cannot reach outside.
The beam slows steadily until it stops beside the astronaut.
The beam moves faster than light to fight gravity.
The flashlight produces no beam once it crosses the horizon.
questions.correctAnswer: The beam moves at light speed nearby, though it cannot reach outside.
questions.explanation: The astronaut still measures light moving at its usual speed. What changes is whether the beam's future path can lead outside.

questions.question: Two probes fire beams directly outward: one is just outside a black hole's event horizon and one is just inside. Which beam can reach a distant telescope?
options: Only the beam from just outside
Only the beam from just inside
Both beams, because both move at light speed
Neither beam, because the horizon blocks all nearby light
questions.correctAnswer: Only the beam from just outside
questions.explanation: An outward-going beam starting outside has a route away. The beam starting inside has no future path across the horizon to the telescope.

questions.question: A probe inside the event horizon cannot send a light signal to its crew outside. It replaces its flashlight with a much brighter laser aimed outward. What changes?
options: It sends more light, but none of that light can reach the crew outside.
The laser's light moves faster and crosses the horizon.
The stronger beam punches a temporary hole through the horizon.
The crew receives the signal because light always moves at light speed.
questions.correctAnswer: It sends more light, but none of that light can reach the crew outside.
questions.explanation: Brightness does not change light's speed or create an escape path. Even an outward-directed signal sent from inside remains inside.
